supersedes: 4.0.0, in full. 4.0.0 judged two composite subjects and left peace-tower, chateau-frontenac and officer explicitly NOT EXAMINED; it also predates the Halifax and Toronto subjects entirely. This record replaces it because it covers every subject that has a render in run 5f188cb9406171fd, and a partial record that reads like a full one is the failure mode this file exists to refuse.

scope.unrenderedIsNotAVerdict: Neither subject was handed over and neither is audited here. Both are UNRENDERED BY DECISION: their renders would be repeating, droppable parallax tiles that the art bible forbids putting an identifying feature on, so a verifier able to name Ottawa or Quebec City from them would be reporting a defect. An audit of an image nobody was shown would be the quietest kind of false pass, and the scorer fails one on purpose.

runIntegrity.blindnessCaveat: partial - see `primingLeak` below. Two identifications are marked partially primed.
whatIsProven: The 37 identifications in `handoffRun.answers` were written from image bytes alone, under opaque 16-hex names, with no filename, label, contract or reference photograph in view.

They were hashed by `verify-art commit` BEFORE `verify-art reveal` opened the keymap, and `score` re-checked the hash against the file on disk. It matched. The blind pass was not revised with the answer key open.

Every source digest in the keymap was re-derived against the tree on the day this record was written and every one matched, so this verdict is about the art that is on disk today and not about a picture that has since been redrawn.
whatIsNotProven: That the identifier read nothing outside the hand-off directory. Only the hand-off can give that, and this record cannot recover it after the fact. What it can say is stated in `primingLeak`.

That the small rungs of the size ladder measure recognition. They do not, and cannot in this hand-off shape: the same identifier saw the full-size render of every subject. See `findings.sizeLadderMeasuresRetentionNotRecognition`.

primingLeak.what: CLAUDE.md is in the identifier's system prompt. It names *Discover Canada*, the IRCC citizenship test, EN/FR, and the recent-commits block names "Build the Ottawa level". So before a single pixel was opened the identifier knew the subjects were Canadian and that Ottawa was among them.
primingLeak.whoseFault: The hand-off's, not the identifier's. It is a structural flaw in how this run was staged.
primingLeak.consequence: The run was not fully open-set. It was open-set as to WHICH Canadian things, and closed as to whether they were Canadian at all.

identificationsConsideredPartiallyPrimed.why: "Build the Ottawa level" in the commit log named the city. A Gothic clock tower with a green copper spire has a strong non-Canadian competitor (Big Ben), and the masked-flag probe's own contract records a hand pass falling to exactly that reading. Weigh the 0.90 accordingly.

Named "Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa" as a best guess while stating in the same answer that "nothing in the picture names it". That is the genre plus the primed city, not a reading of the render - and the contract already accepts the generic answer for exactly this reason, which is why the priming did not change the outcome.

primingLeak.identificationsNotAffected: The Quebec City, Halifax and Toronto subjects. Nothing in the system prompt named those cities or those levels, and the two subjects that failed are in that group.

theQuestionThisRunWasAskedToSettle: For every subject with a render: does an identifier who has never seen the label name the thing, and is every mustBeRight feature actually on the picture?

And specifically, four questions carried over from the blind pass: what the two subjects with nothing identifying in them are asked to be; whether the toboggan lane reads as a built chute and whether its previous neverAdd breach is gone; what the masked probes measure; and what the smallest ladder rung destroys.

results.blindIdentification: The Peace Tower and Centre Block of the Parliament Buildings, Parliament Hill, Ottawa. (0.90)
results.note: Every feature reads. Green spire at 0.19 of tower height, one white dial with four cardinal ticks, flag on the mast, buff sandstone, one Gothic arch on the centre line, symmetrical wings, ~1:7.8. The three tan blocks over the Memorial Arch are a triplet of window heads, not crenellation, and the end pavilion roofs are corner pavilions rather than a flanking twin tower - neither is a neverAdd breach.

Green copper over brick, tower 220x720 = 1:3.27 exactly as measured in the contract, dark slate tower roof against copper wings, cone rhythm, dormer rhythm, rock mass with spruces under a terrace band. No clock, no flag, no heraldry, no snow sheeting the roof planes - the white is on ridges and dormer heads only. The blind answer named the building and separately noted the cliff setting is thin, which is fair: the rock band is ~90 px of a 900 px render.

results.blindIdentification: A Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer in Red Serge full dress - a Mountie. (0.92 on both gating figures)
results.note: The only subject whose eighth feature - identical cartoon proportions - was answerable, because the hand-off carried the comparison figure. Measured on it: same 470 px height, same 540 px shoulder span, same eye line, same hands and feet, six heads; only the costume differs. Sam Browne runs from the wearer's right shoulder to the left hip, which is the correct way round. No badge, no wordmark, no chevrons anywhere.

results.blindIdentification: Skating on a frozen city canal under a road bridge in winter; best guess Rideau Canal Skateway, Ottawa, "but nothing in the picture names it". (0.50)
results.note: Passes on the generic answer the contract was amended to accept, which is the right outcome: the render is two repeating tiles that may not carry a city cue, and the blind answer said so itself. Masonry wall, iron railing, snow banks both sides, curved skate scoring, bridge overhead, ice ramp distinct from snow. Defect noted, not a missing feature: the five skaters' blades rest on the snow-light far bank rather than on the ice band, and only the trailing boot of each carries a blade.

results.blindIdentification: A winter promenade above a snow slide, with people riding wooden toboggans; best guess the Dufferin Terrace glissade, Quebec City, second reading a frozen canal beside a lock. (0.40)
results.note: The redraw worked. The lane is the `snow` ramp throughout, the two dividers are modelled ridges (shaded flank, lit crest, shaded flank) rather than colour-band boundaries, the far timber wall and the near bank close the chute, and four riders sit on flat wooden toboggans. The blind answer read "a snow slide", not a river - which is exactly what the previous pass could not do.

results.blindIdentification: The Old Town Clock on Citadel Hill, Halifax, Nova Scotia. (0.60)
results.note: Cobalt dial with gold hands on a white drum (dial:drum 0.53 against a measured 0.50), green ogee dome under a balustraded cupola and a gold ball, round-arched belfry with two bells, colonnaded gallery wider than every stage above it, white walls on a stone plinth with its arch, turf slope, 1:1.31. The blind answer read the colonnade as running "around the first stage", so the roundness does read even though the gallery rim is drawn straight rather than elliptical.

results.blindIdentification: An ocean-terminal immigration shed: a liner berthed alongside a brick terminal with a boat train on the pier tracks; best guess Pier 21, Halifax. (0.45)
results.note: Passes on the generic answers, which is what this subject is asked for: strip the painted name and Pier 21 is a building type. Three-storey brick block with a stone-coped parapet, streamlined pale entrance with its canopy and pipe rail, low monitor-roofed sheds running off BOTH edges, two-funnel liner with lifeboats and a red band, green heritage coach on rails. No name, no emblem, no clock.

results.blindIdentification: The CN Tower with the Rogers Centre beside it - the Toronto waterfront landmark pair. (0.92)
results.note: The strongest identification in the run and the only one that needed nothing added. Pod at 0.57 of the height, the fat white torus is the pod's widest element, the small upper pod is there, tapering mast, splayed base part-hidden by the dome, dome ~1/7 of the tower height and ~1/3 of it wide. No lattice, no guy wires, no flag, no clock.

results.blindIdentification: "I cannot tell. A generic modern city street with a protected bicycle lane, cyclists, a bike rack, street trees and an anonymous glass-tower skyline behind water." (0.15)
results.note: THE ART IS NOT THE DEFECT. Every mustBeRight feature is on the tile and nothing forbidden is: green and blue lines, white bicycle mark and arrow, verge and kerb, slim young trees, helmeted riders, a skyline of plain masses. Being unable to name a city here is the CORRECT answer - the contract says a verifier who named Toronto from these two repeating tiles "would be reporting a defect, not a pass". It fails on wording: the answer says "a protected bicycle lane", and expectedBlindAnswer carries "a bike lane" and "a cycle track" but no form of the word "bicycle". Recommendation to the contract's owner (art), not a change made here: add "a bicycle lane" and "a protected bicycle lane". Until then this is a real fail and is recorded as one; the frozen answer may not be edited to fit the list.

results.blindIdentification: "A small coastal town's waterfront main street, with a market stall, shops and clapboard houses rising behind, a church steeple and gulls... I cannot name it." (0.20)
results.note: A SUBSTANTIVE MISS, unlike toronto-trail. Every feature is drawn - the planked deck, the timber kerb, lamps, bollards, benches, two slips with a masted hull and a red-banded tug, gabled and dormered waterfront buildings, a monitor-roofed cargo shed, gulls, six figures - and the deck still read as a paved STREET, not a boardwalk, so none of the seven accepted answers was reachable. Being unable to name Halifax is correct and not the failure; failing to read the TYPE is. Cause, for the art agent: the deck is a flat grey field with hairline plank separators and no visible board ends or edge, so at tile scale it reads as asphalt. It is the one place where obeying the contract's own word ("grey weathered planking") produced the wrong read.

twoGenericSubjects.question: The blind pass reported that the bike-lane city street and the small coastal town had nothing identifying at any size, and said this was not a resolution problem. The task asked which one is deliberately generic.
twoGenericSubjects.ruling: BOTH are, and that correction matters. `toronto-trail` and `halifax-quayside` each carry an `expectedBlindAnswerNote` that says GENERIC ON PURPOSE, each is two repeating parallax tiles, and each states where its city identity actually lives instead (`cn-tower` and `town-clock`, both of which passed). Neither is permitted to name a place and neither is asked to. So "nothing identifies a city" is a PASS condition for both, not a defect, and the blind pass was reporting compliance while believing it was reporting a fault.
twoGenericSubjects.andYetBothFail: They fail for two different reasons and only one of them is about art. toronto-trail read as the right TYPE in words the matcher does not carry. halifax-quayside read as the wrong TYPE - a street rather than a boardwalk - and that is a defect in the drawing. Routing them to the same place would waste the art agent's time on the first and hide the second.

theToboggamPromenade.question: The blind pass could not resolve the promenade between two places, called the sideways travel on a flat ice-reading surface a drawing contradiction, and left the built-chute mustBeRight unruled. The subject had also previously breached a neverAdd for a recognisable building on a repeating tile.
theToboggamPromenade.rulingOnTheBuiltChute: PRESENT. The contract does not ask for a view DOWN the run - it says in terms that TrueNorth is a portrait side-scroller and looks ACROSS it, and defines the containment for that camera as a low timber wall with snow capping it along the far side, two straight level lane-divider ridges, and a near snow bank. All three are drawn, and the two dividers are now MODELLED (shaded far flank, lit crest, shaded near flank) rather than the flat colour-band boundaries the previous pass read as a change of water surface. So the sideways travel is not a contradiction; it is the camera the contract specifies. The lane is the `snow` ramp throughout and no longer the `ice` ramp, and the blind answer this run read it as "a snow slide" and "a wide white/pale-blue snow surface" rather than as a river.
theToboggamPromenade.rulingOnThePreviousNeverAddBreach: CLEARED. The striped bandstand kiosk with the green-and-white radial roof and white finial - the one an unprimed verifier named Terrasse Dufferin from, off a tile whose own rule forbids it - is gone. What is there now is a plain open timber shelter with a slate hipped roof. The corroboration is the blind answer itself: it described "a small blue-roofed open pavilion/kiosk" and did not name a place from it. Nothing else on either tile is a named or recognisable building.
theToboggamPromenade.defectFoundWhileRuling: One of the four riders is drawn partly OUTSIDE the slope tile's viewBox and is decapitated at the tile seam: in layer-60-slope.svg its head sits at local y = 1.5 with a toque from y = -21.9 to +2.3, so the rasteriser clips the toque and cuts the head in half against the timber wall. Not a missing mustBeRight feature (three complete riders satisfy the entry) and not a neverAdd breach, so it does not change the verdict - but it is a visible drawing fault and it needs fixing.
theToboggamPromenade.andTheTailOfThatDefect: That toque is drawn in `#a9d0e5`, which is `ice-base`, and 50 pixels of it survive the clip as a two-row sliver at render rows 580-581. It is on the timber wall and not on the lane, and the lane itself carries no ice-ramp pixel at all, so this is NOT scored as the neverAdd breach it nearly is. It matters because the obvious fix - move the rider down into the tile - would bring an ice-ramp garment onto the lane, where the rule does bite. Recolour the toque before moving the rider.

masksMeasureTheProbesAsMuchAsTheArt.observation: The four masked probes fall into two groups and the split is clean. Masking the Chateau's crowning tower took confidence 0.80 -> 0.50 and pushed the answer back to a hedged "a Canadian chateau-style railway hotel"; masking the CN Tower's pod took 0.92 -> 0.70 and the identification then rested on the domed stadium next door rather than on the tower. Masking the Peace Tower's flag took 0.90 -> 0.85 and changed nothing about the reading, and masking the officer's breeches-and-stripe took 0.92 -> 0.80 with the boots taking up the slack.
masksMeasureTheProbesAsMuchAsTheArt.whatItSaysAboutThePROBES: Two of the four masks are load-bearing and two are cheap. A probe that removes a feature the subject does not depend on measures nothing except that the subject does not depend on it - which is worth knowing ONCE and is not worth a gating slot or a place in every future hand-off. The two expensive masks are the ones that turn an assertion in the contract ("the tower is what makes this the Chateau") into a number, and they should stay.
masksMeasureTheProbesAsMuchAsTheArt.whatItSaysAboutTheART: Nothing bad. The Peace Tower result is the good case, not the weak one: the contract's own note records a hand pass where masking the flag collapsed the reading to "a Big Ben-like Gothic clock tower", and this run did not collapse. That is the drawing having got stronger, and it is only visible because the probe was re-run.
masksMeasureTheProbesAsMuchAsTheArt.recommendation: Keep the Chateau and CN Tower masks. Demote the flag and leg-stripe masks to occasional rather than every-run, and record their measured deltas in the contract so the information is not lost by dropping them. This is a note about the probe set and belongs to whoever owns the hand-off recipe, not to the art agent.

sizeLadderMeasuresRetentionNotRecognitio.observation: The landmark silhouettes survive the ladder and the ACTIVITY does not. At 140 px the Peace Tower, the Chateau, the CN Tower, the Town Clock and the officer were all still named. At the same rung the skaters are 6-8 px ticks whose glide pose has gone, the tobogganers are smudges, and both of those subjects fell out: 0/2 diagnostic probes matched for dufferin-terrace-toboggan-run and 0/2 for halifax-quayside, against 3/3 for peace-tower and chateau-frontenac and 5/5 for officer.
sizeLadderMeasuresRetentionNotRecognitio.whatItImpliesForSubjectsBuiltOnPeopleDoi: A subject whose identity is a VERB cannot inherit a landmark's placement floor. A landmark is a silhouette and degrades gracefully into one; an activity is a POSE, and a pose is the first thing a reduction destroys, because it lives in limb angles a few pixels wide. So: the 300 px floor that peace-tower measured and that town-clock, pier-21 and cn-tower ADOPTED without re-deriving is a floor for landmarks only. The skating, tobogganing and boardwalk-walking figures need their own floor, measured on them, and it will be higher. Concretely: skate blades and toboggan runners should be thickened the way the officer's leg stripe already is under its own contract rule ("if it disappears first at small size, thicken it"), and no level should scale a tile whose subject is an activity to a width where its figures fall under about 20 px.
sizeLadderMeasuresRetentionNotRecognitio.caveatOnAllOfIt: This is a RETENTION measurement, not a recognition one, and it must not be quoted as the latter. The same identifier had already seen the full-size render of every subject before it reached the small rungs, so what the ladder shows is how much reduction an answer already formed will survive. Measuring recognition at 140 px needs the small rung to reach someone who has not seen the large one, which is a hand-off SHAPE change and not something any amount of scoring can recover.

onTheFramingOfTheHANDOFF.whatWasDone: Every render was composited onto one 2016x1140 matte at the run's largest extent, because image dimensions were a linkage channel: nine of eleven size classes were subject-pure, so the sizes alone relinked ladder rungs to their full-size renders straight out of answers.json without opening a file.
onTheFramingOfTheHANDOFF.theCostIsReal: It is. A 140x79 drawing parked in the middle of a 2016x1140 grey field is 0.5 per cent of the frame, and every render in the run had to be cropped back to its own extent and point-upscaled locally before anything could be judged. The linkage the matte defeats is also only defeated against a lazy reader: the drawing's extent is still measurable by anyone who opens the image and looks at where the matte stops, which the hand-off's own code comment says plainly.
suggestedAlternative: Pad each render to a canvas drawn from ONE common set of sizes that every subject uses, rather than to a single global maximum. Three or four fixed canvases - say 480x480, 960x960, 1440x1440 - each used by renders from several different subjects, with the assignment chosen so no canvas is subject-pure. That kills the linkage for the same reason the single matte does (the class no longer identifies a subject) while keeping a 140 px drawing inside a 480 px frame instead of a 2016 px one.

The property to hold is not "one size" but "no size class is subject-pure and every class has at least two subjects in it". That is checkable in the harness, and a test that asserts it would say more than the current constant does.

If the single matte is kept, hand over the natural extent as a separate per-render field in answers.json - width/height of the DRAWING, not of the canvas. The identifier already learns it by looking; withholding it costs a crop step per render and hides nothing.
onTheFramingOfTheHANDOFF.whoseCallItIs: Not the identifier's. Recorded here as the requested view, and the trade-off as stated - linkage versus wasted frame - is the right one to be arguing about.

defectsRoutedToArt.what: The boardwalk deck reads as a paved street. It is a flat grey field with hairline plank separators, no board ends, no visible deck edge and no timber warmth, so at tile scale the one feature that makes the subject what it is disappears into road.
defectsRoutedToArt.suggestion: Give the planking a warmer weathered-timber tone and a stronger light/shade rhythm per board, and show the deck EDGE - a board-end line or a fascia under the kerb - so the surface is legibly a structure standing over water rather than ground.

defectsRoutedToArt.severity: visible fault, does not fail the gate
defectsRoutedToArt.what: A rider in layer-60-slope.svg is drawn partly above the tile viewBox and is decapitated at the seam; its toque is clipped away except for a two-row sliver at render rows 580-581.
defectsRoutedToArt.suggestion: Move the rider fully inside the tile - and recolour its toque off `ice-base` first, because on the lane that colour is a neverAdd.

defectsRoutedToArt.what: The skaters' blades rest on the `snow-light` far bank rather than on the ice band, and only the trailing boot of each figure carries a visible blade.
defectsRoutedToArt.suggestion: Drop the figure ground line a few pixels onto the ice, and draw a blade under the supporting boot too. The blade is this subject's equivalent of the officer's leg stripe and the same rule applies to it.

defectsRoutedToArt.what: The gallery roof rim is drawn as a straight band where the reference is elliptical, and the walls carry no clapboard lines, so "white painted wood" rests on colour alone.
defectsRoutedToArt.suggestion: Neither is a missing feature and the blind pass read past both. Worth a pass if the file is open anyway; not worth a redraw on its own.

recommendationsToTheContractOwner.change: Add "a bicycle lane" and "a protected bicycle lane" to expectedBlindAnswer. The list carries "a bike lane" and "a cycle track" and no form of "bicycle", so an answer that names the facility by its ordinary full name fails a gate the art satisfies. Same shape as the amendment rideau-canal-skateway already needed, and found the same way: by an honest answer failing.
recommendationsToTheContractOwner.notMadeHere: references.json is owned by art. This record recommends; it does not edit.

howToReadAFailInThisRecord: Two subjects fail and neither failure is "the drawing is bad everywhere". 64 of 64 mustBeRight features across all ten subjects are present and no neverAdd entry was found anywhere in the run. Both failures are identification failures on subjects that are FORBIDDEN from naming a place, and they are not the same kind: one is a word missing from the contract and one is a surface that reads as the wrong material. Making this file green would have taken one edit to a frozen answers file or one lenient audit line, and either would have been worth less than the two defects it hid.

identifications.answer: A Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officer in Red Serge - a Mountie. Same reading as at full size, still unambiguous at this small scale.
identifications.cues: Red tunic plus tan flat-brimmed Stetson plus navy breeches with a yellow leg stripe plus brown boots - the colour block alone carries it; brown cross-belt and gold buttons just visible.
identifications.moreCertain: More pixels on the hat: at this size the Stetson is close to a generic wide-brim hat, and the yellow leg stripe is only two pixels wide.

identifications.answer: I cannot tell. A generic modern city street with a protected bicycle lane, cyclists, a bike rack, street trees and an anonymous glass-tower skyline behind water. Nothing in it identifies a city, a landmark or anything specifically Canadian.
identifications.cues: A flat-vector skyline of anonymous blue-and-white glass office towers behind a pale band of water; a green verge with round-canopy trees, benches, park-notice boards and curved black lamp standards; three people, two riding bicycles and one standing; a rack of parked bicycles; a roadway across the bottom with a painted cycle lane carrying bicycle pictograms, direction arrows and a blue/green lane tint.
identifications.moreCertain: Any landmark in the skyline, any signage, flag or transit livery. As drawn this could equally be any city in the world; the towers are generic rectangles with window stripes.

identifications.answer: The Old Town Clock, Citadel Hill, Halifax - though a generic 19th-century colonial town hall is an almost equally good reading at this size.
identifications.cues: White tiered tower with columns, blue-and-gold clock face, green copper dome with lantern and gold finial, low white building with dark roof, green lawn.
identifications.moreCertain: Anything Halifax-specific: the Citadel star fort, the harbour, or the tower's characteristic octagonal clock drum rather than a square one.

identifications.answer: The Chateau Frontenac, Quebec City - or at least a Canadian chateau-style railway hotel; at this size I would not bet heavily on which one.
identifications.cues: Green steep copper roofs with conical turrets over red-brick walls, one tall dark-roofed central tower, symmetrical wings, snow and conifers at the base.
identifications.moreCertain: Any silhouette detail unique to the Frontenac - the round tower, the cliff and river, or the terrace - and more pixels on the roofline, which is where all the identity lives.

identifications.answer: A Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officer in Red Serge full dress uniform - a Mountie. Male, dark-skinned, standing at ease.
identifications.cues: Scarlet red high-collar tunic with a row of brass buttons; tan felt broad-brimmed Stetson campaign hat with a flat brim and hat band; brown leather Sam Browne belt with a diagonal cross-strap over the right shoulder; dark navy breeches with a yellow-gold stripe down the outside seam; high brown riding boots; white lanyard at the shoulder; two flapped breast pockets.
identifications.moreCertain: A legible RCMP cap badge / collar insignia, and the yellow-brown shoulder strap on the Stetson; the tunic collar reads plain at this size.

identifications.answer: Two full-body cartoon NPCs side by side. Right: a female RCMP officer in Red Serge (a Mountie) - confident. Left: I cannot tell what she is meant to be. A smiling young woman with dark shoulder-length hair in a plain green zip-up jacket with a blank white/pale rounded panel on the chest, blue jeans and tan boots. The blank panel reads as an unfilled name badge or logo patch, so her role is not identifiable; possible readings include a park/Parks Canada guide, a volunteer or simply a civilian townsfolk character.
identifications.cues: Right figure: scarlet tunic, tan Stetson, brown Sam Browne cross-strap, navy breeches with yellow stripe, brown riding boots. Left figure: green jacket with a white zip line and a blank white chest panel, jeans, work boots, no hat, no tool, no insignia of any kind.
identifications.moreCertain: For the left figure: any legible insignia, logo or lettering on that white chest panel, or a prop (radio, clipboard, hat, backpack) that names her job. As drawn, nothing distinguishes her from a generic civilian.

identifications.answer: A winter promenade above a snow slide, with people riding wooden toboggans. My best guess is the toboggan slide (glissade) on Dufferin Terrace beside the Chateau Frontenac in Quebec City; my second reading is a frozen canal beside a lock, with the timber structure as a lock gate. I am not confident between them.
identifications.cues: A raised promenade with an ornate dark-green cast-iron railing of pointed lyre-shaped panels; white globe lamps on green posts; a small blue-roofed open pavilion/kiosk with two attendants inside; public benches with people standing at them; a stone/concrete retaining wall below the promenade; a heavy timber gantry with a planked walkway on top and diagonal X-bracing straddling the scene; below, a wide white/pale-blue snow surface with long streak lines on which three people sit on wooden slat toboggans.
identifications.moreCertain: What the timber gantry is meant to be. As drawn it could be a toboggan-slide launch tower or a canal lock gate, and those two readings give completely different places. Also, the riders sit on toboggans yet slide sideways across the frame on what reads as flat ice, which fights the slide interpretation.

identifications.answer: A Canadian chateau-style railway hotel; my best guess is the Chateau Frontenac, Quebec City, but I am much less sure here. The top of the central tower - its steep dark roof, dormers and finial - has been painted out, leaving the middle block ending in a flat blank top, which removes the building's main vertical signature.
identifications.cues: Green copper roofs with dormers, conical corner turrets, red-brick walls with stone trim, arcaded ground floor with a central arched entrance, snowy ground with conifers. Against it: no crowning tower, so the outline reads closer to a generic grand hotel.
identifications.moreCertain: The masked-out central tower roof. It is the feature that makes this building itself rather than any chateau-style hotel, and without it I was choosing between Frontenac, Banff Springs and Chateau Laurier on colour alone.

identifications.answer: The Peace Tower and Centre Block, Parliament Hill, Ottawa. Note: no flag is flying from the tower in this version - the mast/flag appears to have been removed or painted out.
identifications.cues: Tall pale-limestone Gothic Revival clock tower with a green copper spire and corner pinnacles; white clock face with black hands high on the tower; long symmetrical wing either side with a row of pointed Gothic arched windows and a continuous green copper roof with dormers/finials; a separate slim dark conical spire to the right of the tower (reads as the Library of Parliament roof); arched central entrance at the tower base; conifers along the front lawn. Absence of the flag did not change the reading; the tower proportion, the clock and the green copper roofline are enough.
identifications.moreCertain: Restoring the flag would have made it instant; without it I checked the tower silhouette and the Library cone before committing.

identifications.answer: The CN Tower with the Rogers Centre (SkyDome) beside it - the Toronto waterfront skyline landmark pair.
identifications.cues: Very tall slender tapered concrete shaft; a main pod near the top made of a dark banded observation level sitting on a white saucer/restaurant disc; a smaller pod (SkyPod) higher up the shaft; a thin antenna mast above that; immediately beside its base a low white domed stadium with a colonnaded ring, reading as a retractable-roof ballpark; a small tree and a low blue-glass building alongside.
identifications.moreCertain: Nothing needed; the tower-plus-dome pairing is decisive. A hint of the tower's tripod/leg flare at the base would be the only refinement.

identifications.answer: The Peace Tower and Centre Block, Parliament Hill, Ottawa.
identifications.cues: Tall pale-limestone Gothic Revival clock tower with a green copper spire and corner pinnacles; white clock face with black hands high on the tower; long symmetrical wing either side with a row of pointed Gothic arched windows and a continuous green copper roof with dormers/finials; a separate slim dark conical spire to the right of the tower (reads as the Library of Parliament roof); arched central entrance at the tower base; conifers along the front lawn. Canadian maple leaf flag on the mast above the spire.
identifications.moreCertain: Nothing much - it survives this reduction well. A slightly larger clock face would help; the hands are almost gone.

identifications.answer: A Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officer in Red Serge - a Mountie. The hips/thighs are covered by a blank grey rectangle, so the breeches and leg stripe are not visible; the identification does not depend on them.
identifications.cues: Scarlet tunic with brass buttons; tan Stetson; brown Sam Browne belt with diagonal cross-strap; white lanyard; brown riding boots below the masked band.
identifications.moreCertain: Seeing the breeches and the yellow leg stripe that the mask removes - without them the uniform could be argued as another ceremonial red tunic (e.g. a bandsman), and the boots are what pull it back.

identifications.answer: The CN Tower and the Rogers Centre (SkyDome), Toronto.
identifications.cues: Very tall slender tapered concrete shaft; a main pod near the top made of a dark banded observation level sitting on a white saucer/restaurant disc; a smaller pod (SkyPod) higher up the shaft; a thin antenna mast above that; immediately beside its base a low white domed stadium with a colonnaded ring, reading as a retractable-roof ballpark; a small tree and a low blue-glass building alongside.
identifications.moreCertain: At this size the two pods start to merge into one blob; a touch more separation between the SkyPod and the main pod would hold up better.

identifications.answer: The Old Town Clock (Halifax Town Clock) on Citadel Hill, Halifax, Nova Scotia.
identifications.cues: Three-stage white tower stepping back as it rises, on top of a low white one-storey building with a dark hipped roof; a colonnade of slim white columns around the first stage; a deep blue clock face with gold hands and gold hour marks; above it an open belfry stage with arched openings and gold bells; a green copper dome capped by a small white lantern with a gold ball finial; grassy slope in front and a stone base with a low arch.
identifications.moreCertain: The real Town Clock has four clock faces on an irregular octagonal drum and sits on a much narrower Palladian base; here the base is a wide plain hall and the tower is square, so it also reads as a generic colonial town hall or courthouse. The grassy slope of Citadel Hill and a glimpse of the ramparts would settle it.

identifications.answer: Skating on a frozen city canal under a road bridge in winter. My best guess at a named place is the Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa, but nothing in the picture names it; it could be any frozen urban waterway.
identifications.cues: A long flat ribbon of pale blue ice with wind-streak lines running the full width, between snow banks; five figures in winter coats, toques and mitts in skating poses, one leg trailing; a small wooden hut with a snow-covered roof on the bank (reads as a warming/skate-change hut); a concrete road bridge with a guarded parapet and heavy piers crossing overhead; snow-capped conifers; period-style lamp standards with gold globe lamps along the bank.
identifications.moreCertain: One identifying landmark on the bank - Parliament, the Chateau Laurier, the flight of Ottawa Locks, or a BeaverTails-style stall - or signage. As drawn, the bridge and hut are generic.

identifications.answer: I cannot tell. A generic downtown street with a bike lane, cyclists, benches, trees and a nondescript glass skyline. No identifiable place.
identifications.cues: Bicycle pictograms and arrows painted on the road, cyclists and a bike rack on the verge, round trees and lamp posts, rectangular towers behind a strip of water.
identifications.moreCertain: A recognisable building or sign anywhere in the skyline, or a distinctive piece of street furniture.

identifications.answer: Winter skating on a frozen canal or river beneath a road bridge; probably intended as the Rideau Canal Skateway, Ottawa, but unnamed by anything in frame.
identifications.cues: Broad ice sheet with streak marks, small skating figures in coats and toques, wooden hut on the snowy bank, concrete bridge overhead, lamp posts, snowy conifers.
identifications.moreCertain: A named landmark in the background; also the skaters are now barely more than coloured ticks and one could read them as walkers.

identifications.answer: The CN Tower and the Rogers Centre (SkyDome), Toronto.
identifications.cues: Needle-thin tapered tower with a bulge near the top and a mast above it, standing directly beside a white dome - the silhouette alone is enough.
identifications.moreCertain: The upper SkyPod has almost vanished and the main pod is a smear; only the overall silhouette survives.

identifications.answer: An ocean-terminal immigration shed: a passenger liner berthed alongside a brick terminal building with a boat train waiting on the pier tracks. My best guess is Pier 21 in Halifax, the immigration gateway, though nothing in frame names it.
identifications.cues: An ocean liner alongside at left: white superstructure with rows of dark windows, two buff-and-black funnels, a dark hull with a red boot line and a row of white lifeboats under davits, a mast forward; a red-brick terminal building centre with tall multi-pane windows, a wide white portal/canopy over the ground floor and a dark doorway; a railway track running along the foreground with a dark green wooden-bodied passenger/colonist car with a yellow band and a stove chimney standing right at the building; a low white shed with a dark roof at right, also on the tracks.
identifications.moreCertain: Signage or the Pier 21 name; the long low corrugated shed shape of the real Pier 21 rather than a three-storey brick block; or immigrants with trunks and luggage on the platform, which would fix the subject as arrival rather than a generic port.

identifications.answer: A small seaside town street with shops, market stalls, houses on a slope, a church steeple and gulls. I cannot say which town; a Maritime Canadian fishing town is a guess from the gulls and the clapboard housing, not a reading.
identifications.cues: Gulls, clapboard gabled houses in pastel colours, white church tower with a spire, awninged shopfront, market stall and benches, small figures along a promenade.
identifications.moreCertain: A landmark, a boat, a harbour or signage; the setting is generic and at this size the houses are just coloured rectangles with triangles on top.

identifications.answer: A female Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officer in Red Serge - a Mountie.
identifications.cues: Red tunic, tan flat-brimmed Stetson, brown cross-belt and wide belt with a gold buckle, navy breeches with a yellow stripe, brown riding boots.
identifications.moreCertain: More pixels: at this size the Stetson brim and the belt buckle are only a few pixels and the face reads as a blur.

identifications.answer: The Peace Tower and Centre Block, Parliament Hill, Ottawa.
identifications.cues: Green-spired square clock tower over a long arcaded pale stone building with a green copper roof; red-and-white maple leaf flag above the spire; small dark cone to the right; central arched doorway.
identifications.moreCertain: The clock face has dissolved into a grey speckle at this size and the Gothic window heads have gone soft - the flag is doing a lot of the identification work.

identifications.answer: The CN Tower and the Rogers Centre (SkyDome), Toronto. In this version the main pod has been mostly painted out - only the white saucer underside remains and the dark banded observation deck and the shaft immediately above it are missing, so the tower has a broken/floating look.
identifications.cues: Tapered concrete shaft, white saucer disc partway up, upper SkyPod and antenna mast still present, white domed stadium at the base, low blue-glass block beside it.
identifications.moreCertain: The removed observation pod is the tower's signature feature; with it gone I leaned heavily on the dome next door. On the tower by itself I would have been much less sure.

identifications.answer: A white clock tower with a green dome over a low white colonial building. My best guess is the Old Town Clock, Halifax, but at this size I honestly cannot rule out a generic town hall or courthouse.
identifications.cues: Green dome with gold finial, blue clock disc with gold hands, white columned stage, dark hipped roof over a white hall, strip of grass.
identifications.moreCertain: More pixels: the belfry bells and the column spacing have collapsed into blocks, and those are the details that make it a specific building rather than a generic one.

identifications.answer: A frozen waterway in winter with a few tiny figures on the ice and a bridge across the top - a skating scene. I cannot tell what specific place it is; Rideau Canal Skateway is a guess, not a reading.
identifications.cues: Large pale ice band, snow bank, small dark figures, concrete bridge with piers, lamp standards, conifers.
identifications.moreCertain: At this size the skaters are 6-8 pixels tall and their skating pose is gone; a stronger silhouette or a larger warming hut would carry the activity better.

identifications.answer: A Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officer in Red Serge full dress - a Mountie. Female, light-skinned, auburn hair.
identifications.cues: Scarlet red high-collar tunic with a row of brass buttons; tan felt broad-brimmed Stetson campaign hat with a flat brim and hat band; brown leather Sam Browne belt with a diagonal cross-strap over the right shoulder; dark navy breeches with a yellow-gold stripe down the outside seam; high brown riding boots; white lanyard at the shoulder; two flapped breast pockets.
identifications.moreCertain: A legible cap badge or collar insignia; the mouth shape is odd (reads as a small white oval) which briefly distracted me from the uniform.

identifications.answer: People riding wooden toboggans below an ornate green-railed winter boardwalk with globe lamps and a kiosk. Probably the Dufferin Terrace toboggan slide, Quebec City, but I cannot tell for certain; a canal-side promenade is an equally live reading.
identifications.cues: Green cast-iron railing with white globe lamps, blue-roofed kiosk with attendants, benches and onlookers, timber gantry with X-bracing, seated figures on slat toboggans on a white snow/ice surface.
identifications.moreCertain: A landmark above the terrace - the Chateau Frontenac roofline would have made this unmistakable - or a slide angled downhill rather than a flat horizontal run.

identifications.answer: A winter scene: figures on small sleds on snow below a railed promenade with lamps, a kiosk and a wooden gantry. I cannot tell what place this is meant to be.
identifications.cues: Green railing band with white globe lamps, small blue-roofed hut, tan timber frame with X-bracing, three tiny seated figures on sleds, broad white ground.
identifications.moreCertain: At this size the toboggans read as smudges and the railing pattern is gone; the activity itself is barely legible, let alone the location.

identifications.answer: The Peace Tower and Centre Block of the Parliament Buildings, Parliament Hill, Ottawa.
identifications.cues: Tall pale-limestone Gothic Revival clock tower with a green copper spire and corner pinnacles; white clock face with black hands high on the tower; long symmetrical wing either side with a row of pointed Gothic arched windows and a continuous green copper roof with dormers/finials; a separate slim dark conical spire to the right of the tower (reads as the Library of Parliament roof); arched central entrance at the tower base; conifers along the front lawn. Canadian red-and-white maple leaf flag flying from the tower mast.
identifications.moreCertain: The Centre Block wings are drawn very plain and repetitive; a hint of the Library's polygonal buttressed form rather than a bare cone would have removed my last doubt.

identifications.answer: The Chateau Frontenac, Quebec City.
identifications.cues: Massive chateau-style hotel: red-orange brick walls with pale stone quoins and banding; very steep green copper roofs studded with dormers; conical corner turrets with finials; a tall central tower block carrying a steep dark slate roof with dormers and a spike finial; a ground-floor arcade of tall arched openings with a larger arched central entrance; set on a snowy bluff with conifers.
identifications.moreCertain: Same as above, plus the dormers and turret finials are getting mushy here; the roof pitch is what still reads.

identifications.answer: I cannot tell. A city street with a cycle lane and a generic skyline, reduced to the point where only the bike pictograms and the tower blocks are readable.
identifications.cues: White bicycle glyphs on a dark road strip, small figures with bicycles, green verge with trees, blue-grey towers.
identifications.moreCertain: It is not a size problem so much as a content problem - there is nothing specific in the full-size version either.

identifications.answer: The Chateau Frontenac, Quebec City.
identifications.cues: Massive chateau-style hotel: red-orange brick walls with pale stone quoins and banding; very steep green copper roofs studded with dormers; conical corner turrets with finials; a tall central tower block carrying a steep dark slate roof with dormers and a spike finial; a ground-floor arcade of tall arched openings with a larger arched central entrance; set on a snowy bluff with conifers.
identifications.moreCertain: Chateau-style railway hotels are a family (Banff Springs, Chateau Laurier, Fort Garry). The brick-and-copper colouring and the single dominant central tower point to Frontenac, but the Frontenac's round Citadel-side tower and its cliff-top setting over the St Lawrence are not shown, and there is no Dufferin Terrace below it.

identifications.answer: A small coastal town's waterfront main street, with a market stall, shops and clapboard houses rising behind, a church steeple and gulls. It feels like an Atlantic Canada / Maritimes town - Lunenburg or a Newfoundland outport are the sort of thing - but I cannot name it and nothing in frame identifies it.
identifications.cues: A waterfront street in the foreground with a market stall, crates, benches, waste bins, lamp posts and half a dozen townsfolk; a dark timber shop front with an awning and a notice board; behind it clapboard gabled houses in white, blue and terracotta stacked up a slope with a white church tower and steeple among them; seagulls perched on the lamps and flying; a pale water/sky band behind.
identifications.moreCertain: A named landmark or a distinctive local building - Lunenburg's Academy or its bright painted waterfront warehouses, jellybean row colouring, fishing boats and stages, or signage. The houses here are generic clapboard shapes.

identifications.answer: A female Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officer in Red Serge - a Mountie. A blank grey rectangle covers the hips and thighs, hiding the breeches and leg stripe.
identifications.cues: Scarlet tunic with brass buttons and flapped breast pockets; tan Stetson; brown Sam Browne cross-strap and belt; white lanyard; brown riding boots below the mask.
identifications.moreCertain: The masked-out breeches with the yellow stripe - they are the second-strongest cue after the tunic, and losing them leaves the Stetson doing most of the work.

identifications.answer: A waterfront scene with a large steamship, a brick building and a green railway carriage on tracks. I cannot tell what specific place it is meant to be; a port immigration terminal is the best I can say.
identifications.cues: Two funnels and a white liner superstructure, brick facade with a white portal, green railcar with a yellow stripe, rails in the foreground.
identifications.moreCertain: More pixels - at this size the lifeboats and the carriage windows are single-pixel rows - and something in frame that names the port.

identifications.answer: A ship, a brick terminal building and a railway carriage at a pier - a port arrival/immigration terminal. Best guess Pier 21, Halifax; I cannot confirm it.
identifications.cues: Two-funnelled liner with lifeboats, brick building with a white arched entrance canopy, green wooden passenger car on rails, white shed at right.
identifications.moreCertain: Any labelling, or people with luggage; the three elements are recognisable but the specific place is not.

identifications.answer: A town street with shops and stacked houses behind, and small figures on a pavement. I cannot tell what place it is meant to be, and at this size I can barely tell it is coastal.
identifications.cues: Rows of gabled rooftops in pale blue, white and terracotta, one white steeple, a dark shopfront, small human figures, lamp posts.
identifications.moreCertain: More pixels, and a defining feature - a harbour, boats or a named building. The gulls that hinted at a coast in the larger version have disappeared entirely here.

ramp on the toboggan lane, the absence of a <text> element - the SVG source was read as well.
